s: What is the minimum capacity for a solar park to be called an Ultra Mega Solar Park?
x: An Ultra Mega Solar Park has a capacity of 500 MW or more at one location.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about floating solar power in India?
o: India's estimated floating-solar potential is about 102 GW
Omkareshwar is the largest identified floating solar project
Existing floating-solar capacity is about 0.7 GW
The 278 MW Omkareshwar project is in Andhra Pradesh
x: The 278 MW Omkareshwar project is in Madhya Pradesh.

s:
Consider the following statements about MNRE's Solar Park Scheme:
1. It was launched on 12 December 2014.
2. It gives CFA of ₹25 lakh per park for preparing the DPR.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the scheme dates from 12 December 2014 and gives ₹25 lakh per park for the DPR plus up to ₹20 lakh/MW or 30% of cost.

s: The largest floating solar plant in India, Omkareshwar (278 MW), is in which state?
x: Omkareshwar on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh is India's largest floating solar plant, not one in AP.

s: Which solar park of Andhra Pradesh was once the world's largest single-location solar park?
x: The 1,000 MW Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park at Gani-Sakunala was once the world's largest single-location solar park.

s: The 1,000 MW Ultra Mega Solar Park at Gani-Sakunala, Panyam mandal, is in which district?
x: The Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park (1,000 MW) is at Gani-Sakunala, Panyam mandal, Kurnool district (APPSC 2019).

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Kadapa Ultra Mega Solar Park — Galiveedu
x: Ananthapuram-I Solar Park is located at NP Kunta, not Galiveedu. Galiveedu is the location of Kadapa Ultra Mega Solar Park.

s: The Hybrid Solar-Wind Park at Ramagiri is in which district of Andhra Pradesh?
x: Ramagiri hybrid solar-wind park is in Ananthapuramu (APPSC 2023).

s: Galiveedu is the site of which solar park?
x: Galiveedu in YSR Kadapa hosts the 1,000 MW Kadapa Ultra Mega Solar Park; NP Kunta is Ananthapuram-I.

s: Where is NTPC's 25 MW floating solar plant in Andhra Pradesh, operational from 1 July 2022?
x: NTPC's 25 MW floating solar plant at Simhadri, Visakhapatnam, began operation on 1 July 2022.

s: In which village is the Ultra Mega Solar Park-II of Ananthapuramu district located?
x: Ultra Mega Solar Park-II is at Talaricheruvu in Ananthapuramu; NP Kunta has Ananthapuram-I.

s: Where is the 1,500 MW Ananthapuram-I Solar Park located?
x: The 1,500 MW Ananthapuram-I Solar Park is at NP Kunta in Ananthapuramu district.

s: What are the approximate shares of solar and wind, respectively, in Andhra Pradesh's renewable capacity of 10,639.75 MW?
x: Solar energy accounts for approximately 53% and wind energy for approximately 41% of Andhra Pradesh’s renewable-energy mix of 10,639.75 MW.

s: Why did Andhra Pradesh's coal-based power generation face difficulty after bifurcation?
o: A ban on new thermal power plants
Closure of its ports to imported coal
Transfer of its thermal plants to the Centre
Loss of coal mines, leading to long coal haulage and poor coal quality
x: Andhra Pradesh lost its coal mines after bifurcation, causing long coal haulage and exposure to poor coal quality.

s: As on 31 March 2026, what was Andhra Pradesh's rank among States in total renewable energy capacity including large hydro?
x: AP's 15,980 MW put it 6th, after Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.

s: Which state leads India in installed solar capacity (31 March 2026)?
x: Rajasthan leads in solar, while Gujarat leads in total RE and wind; AP is 6th in each.

s: Which state leads India in total renewable energy capacity and in wind capacity (31 March 2026)?
x: Gujarat leads total RE and wind; Rajasthan leads solar.

s: In 2025-26 Andhra Pradesh added about how much renewable energy capacity?
x: AP added 3,865.63 MW of RE in 2025-26, nearly four times the 1,085.15 MW of 2024-25.

s: As on 31 March 2026, what was Andhra Pradesh's approximate share in India's total renewable energy capacity including large hydro?
x: AP had about 15,980 MW of RE including large hydro, about 5.8% of India's 274.7 GW, ranking 6th.

s: What is the estimated wind power potential of Andhra Pradesh at 150 metres above ground level?
x: NIWE estimates AP's wind potential at about 74.9 GW at 120 m and about 123.33 GW at 150 m.

s: What is the solar power potential of Andhra Pradesh as estimated by the National Institute of Solar Energy?
x: NISE estimated AP's solar potential at about 38.44 GWp (Census 2011 based; India total about 749 GWp).

s: Where is the 400 MW wind component of the Tata Renewable 800 MW hybrid project in Andhra Pradesh?
x: The project combines 400 MW solar at Pathikonda (Kurnool) with 400 MW wind at Kanekallu (Anantapur).

s: The 400 MW solar component of the Tata Renewable hybrid project in AP is located in which district?
x: Its 400 MW solar part is at Pathikonda in Kurnool; the wind part is at Kanekallu in Anantapur.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Tata Renewable hybrid project in Andhra Pradesh?
o: It has 400 MW of solar at Pathikonda
It has 400 MW of wind at Kanekallu
x: The project has 400 MW solar at Pathikonda (Kurnool) and 400 MW wind at Kanekallu (Anantapur).

s: Which companies agreed in August 2025 to build a 700 MW wind project in Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh's first wind project since 2019?
x: Tata Power and Suzlon agreed on a ₹6,000 crore, 700 MW wind project in Anantapur, the first in AP since 2019.

s: The ₹6,000 crore wind project announced by Tata Power and Suzlon in August 2025 is in which district of Andhra Pradesh?
x: The 700 MW Tata Power–Suzlon wind project is in Anantapur, a major wind district of AP.

s: The 600 MW SAEL solar project in Kadapa was the first project commissioned under which Andhra Pradesh policy?
o: Andhra Pradesh Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy, 2023
x: The 600 MW SAEL project in Kadapa is identified as a development under the Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024 (ICEP-2024).

s: For what purpose did Andhra Pradesh open 50,000 acres of barren land for solar leases?
x: The barren land was opened for solar leases to avoid diversion of farmland for renewable-energy projects.

s: Which agency is the nodal agency for the AP Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy, 2023?
x: NREDCAP, the State nodal agency for renewable energy, is the nodal agency of the 2023 Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy.

s: Andhra Pradesh's Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targets how much new renewable energy capacity by 2029?
x: ICEP-2024 targets 160 GW of new RE by 2029, including 78.5 GW solar and 35 GW wind.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Integrated Clean Energy Policy (ICEP) 2024 of Andhra Pradesh:
1. It targets 22 GW of pumped storage.
2. It targets 1.5 MTPA of green hydrogen.
3. It aims at net zero by 2047.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are ICEP-2024 targets: 22 GW pumped storage, 25 GWh BESS, 1.5 MTPA green hydrogen and net zero by 2047.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Srisailam Right Bank hydel — APPDCL — Kurnool
x: Simhadri STPS at Visakhapatnam is operated by NTPC and has a capacity of 2,000 MW. Krishnapatnam is operated by APPDCL, while Dr NTTPS and Srisailam Right Bank hydel are associated with APGENCO.

s: Which company operates the 2,400 MW Krishnapatnam SDSTPS in Nellore district?
x: Krishnapatnam SDSTPS (2,400 MW) is run by APPDCL.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
x: Simhadri STPS is operated by NTPC; the other three are APGENCO plants.

s: Which company operates the Simhadri Super Thermal Power Station near Visakhapatnam?
x: Simhadri STPS (2,000 MW) is an NTPC plant, not APGENCO.

s: Where is the Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant of APGENCO located?
x: The Rayalaseema TPP of APGENCO is at Muddanur in Kadapa district; Dr NTTPS is at Ibrahimpatnam near Vijayawada.

s: What is the combined thermal capacity of APGENCO's Dr NTTPS and Rayalaseema TPP?
x: APGENCO's two thermal plants, Dr NTTPS (Vijayawada) and RTPP (Muddanur), together have 4,210 MW.

s: Where is the Dr Narla Tatarao Thermal Power Station (Dr NTTPS) of APGENCO located?
x: Dr NTTPS is at Ibrahimpatnam near Vijayawada and is run by APGENCO.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: On-stream pumped-storage potential of India – about 209 GW
Off-stream pumped-storage potential of India – about 58 GW
Installed pumped-storage capacity of India – about 7 GW
Installed pumped-storage capacity of India – about 58 GW
x: India's installed pumped-storage capacity is about 7 GW; its potential is about 58 GW on-stream and 209 GW off-stream.

s: The Pinnapuram Integrated Renewable Energy Storage Project, developed by Greenko, is in which district?
x: Pinnapuram IRESP, combining solar, wind and pumped storage, is in Kurnool and developed by Greenko.

s: The Gandikota pumped storage project, developed by Adani Green, is in which district?
x: Gandikota PSP is in YSR Kadapa district, developed by Adani Green.

s: What is Andhra Pradesh's estimated pumped-storage potential?
x: AP's PSP potential is about 42,020 MW, among the leading states.

s: What is India's total pumped-storage potential?
x: National PSP potential is about 267 GW: 58 GW on-stream plus 209 GW off-stream.

s: Which agency functions as the State nodal agency for renewable energy in Andhra Pradesh and handles land, clearances and single-window facilitation?
x: NREDCAP is the State nodal agency for renewable energy and facilitates land, clearances and single-window services.

s: Which agency is mainly associated with energy conservation in Andhra Pradesh?
x: APSECM is the agency associated with energy conservation.

s: For what are APGENCO and APPDCL mainly responsible in Andhra Pradesh?
x: APGENCO/APPDCL handle state generation (thermal, hydel, solar); NREDCAP is RE nodal and APSECM handles conservation.

s: What is the target number of farm pumps under PM-KUSUM in Andhra Pradesh?
x: PM-KUSUM in Andhra Pradesh targets 2.93 lakh farm pumps. The figure of 32,000 refers to solar pumps installed earlier.

s: Under PM Surya Ghar in Andhra Pradesh, rooftop solar for about 20.5 lakh households is aimed at which group?
x: About 20.5 lakh SC/ST households (~2 kW each) are covered, with Virtual Net Metering for about 16 lakh.

s: Which arrangement lets about 16 lakh SC/ST households in AP benefit from solar under PM Surya Ghar without own rooftop panels?
x: Virtual Net Metering is planned for about 16 lakh SC/ST households at a lease of about ₹200 a month.

s:
Assertion (A): An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature.
Reason (R): An ecosystem consists of biotic and abiotic components.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true: an ecosystem is a working unit of nature because its living and non-living parts interact. R explains A.

s: Which of the following is open for energy but nearly closed for matter?
x: The Earth receives energy from outside but is nearly closed for matter; ecosystems are open for both energy and matter.

s: The rate of decomposition is likely to be fastest under which of the following conditions?
o: Detritus rich in nitrogen and sugars, with a warm and moist climate
Detritus rich in chitin, with cold and dry conditions
Detritus rich in lignin, with low temperature and anaerobic conditions
Detritus poor in nitrogen, with persistent waterlogging
x: Decomposition is rapid when detritus contains nitrogen and sugars and the climate is warm and moist. Lignin, chitin, low temperature and anaerobic conditions slow it down.

s: Which one of the following represents a functional process of an ecosystem rather than its structure?
x: Nutrient cycling is an ecosystem function. Species composition, trophic levels and abiotic materials are elements of ecosystem structure.

s: An abiotic factor is best defined as which one of the following?
o: An organism that obtains food from dead organic matter
Any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment
A living component occupying the highest trophic level
A biological interaction between two species
x: An abiotic factor is any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment, such as light, temperature, water or soil.

s: Which of the following describes saprotrophs?
x: Saprotrophs feed on dead matter; reptiles are cold-blooded, humans omnivores and camels desert-adapted.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about producers in ecosystems?
o: At deep-sea vents, chemosynthetic sulphur bacteria are the producers
In aquatic ecosystems, zooplankton are the main producers
In terrestrial ecosystems, herbs, shrubs and trees are producers
In aquatic ecosystems, phytoplankton and algae are producers
x: Zooplankton are primary consumers; aquatic producers are phytoplankton, algae and submerged and floating plants.

s: Chemoautotrophic bacteria in deep ocean trenches obtain energy by oxidising which substance released from sea-floor cracks?
x: Chemoautotrophic bacteria in deep ocean trenches use hydrogen sulphide released from sea-floor cracks as an energy source.

s: Why are decomposers regarded as a link between the biotic and abiotic components?
o: Convert dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients reused by producers
Prevent nutrient cycling in the soil
x: Decomposers release inorganic nutrients from dead organic matter, making them available again to producers and linking living and non-living components.

s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: Cyanobacteria – Photosynthetic prokaryotes, many fixing nitrogen
Methanogens – Anaerobic wetlands and ruminant digestive tract
x: Protists are unicellular eukaryotes of water and moist places, some parasitic.

s: What kind of system is an ecosystem, which exchanges energy and matter with its surroundings?
x: An ecosystem is an open system, made of abiotic parts, producers, consumers and decomposers.

s: Through which of the following does a biogeochemical cycle move nutrients?
x: Nutrients cycle through both the living (biotic) and the non-living (abiotic) parts of an ecosystem.

s: Which of the following is true of an ecosystem?
o: It cycles nutrients and has its own productivity
It has a fixed universal boundary
x: An ecosystem cycles nutrients, has its own productivity and has no fixed universal boundary.

s: With which of the following is free-living Azotobacter associated?
x: Azotobacter fixes atmospheric nitrogen.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Photoautotrophs — Chemical oxidation as the energy source
Chemoautotrophs — Sunlight as the energy source
Photoautotrophs — Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria
Archaea — All members depend on photosynthesis
x: Photoautotrophs use sunlight and include green plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Chemoautotrophs obtain energy through chemical oxidation, while many archaea are chemoautotrophic.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the components of an ecosystem?
o: Fire and gravity may function as abiotic factors
Parasites and symbionts are abiotic components
Topography and wind are abiotic components
x: Parasites and symbionts are living, biotic components.

s: Which law states that growth is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply?
x: Liebig's law; Shelford's law of tolerance says both too little and too much of a factor can limit an organism.

s:
Which of the following is the correct sequence of decomposition processes?

1. Fragmentation
2. Leaching
3. Catabolism
4. Humification
5. Mineralisation
x: Decomposition proceeds through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.

s: Who are the principal decomposers in an ecosystem?
x: Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers whose enzymes carry out catabolism; earthworms, nematodes and arthropods are helpers.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Lions are tertiary consumers when they feed on other carnivores such as wolves. They are not primary consumers, which feed directly on producers.

s: Which biogeochemical cycle begins with rock weathering?
x: The phosphorus cycle starts with rock weathering; the water cycle is driven by solar energy.

s: A biogeochemical cycle refers to the movement of which of the following?
x: A biogeochemical cycle moves chemical elements (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus) between living things and the environment. Energy flows one way and does not cycle.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes macroconsumers from microconsumers?
o: Macroconsumers are phagotrophs, whereas microconsumers are saprotrophs.
Macroconsumers are abiotic, whereas microconsumers are biotic.
Macroconsumers manufacture inorganic nutrients, whereas microconsumers consume sunlight.
Macroconsumers are decomposers, whereas microconsumers are herbivores.
x: Macroconsumers, or phagotrophs, ingest food particles or organisms. Microconsumers, or saprotrophs, obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter.

s: In which year did A.G. Tansley coin the term 'ecosystem'?
x: Tansley coined 'ecosystem' in 1935; Haeckel coined 'ecology' in 1866 and Suess 'biosphere' in 1875.

s: Which law states that both too little and too much of a factor can limit an organism?
x: Shelford's Law of Tolerance says both deficiency and excess limit; Liebig's law concerns the nutrient in shortest supply.

s: Altitude, slope and aspect are which type of abiotic factors?
x: Altitude, slope and aspect are topographic; soil factors are edaphic and light, temperature, rainfall are climatic.

s: Methanogens, which are chemoautotrophs, belong to which group?
x: Many archaea, such as methanogens, are chemoautotrophs; cyanobacteria are photoautotrophs.

s: Energy flow and nutrient cycling are aspects of which of the following?
x: Ecosystem function includes processes such as energy flow and nutrient cycling, which support productivity and services.

s: In the carbon cycle, which process takes up CO₂ from the atmosphere?
x: Photosynthesis takes up CO₂, while respiration, decay and combustion release it.

s: Producers, consumers and decomposers together form which aspect of an ecosystem?
x: Producers, consumers and decomposers form the structure of an ecosystem; the food chain is its dynamic (functional) part.

s: What are organisms that can tolerate only a narrow range of temperature called?
x: Stenothermal organisms tolerate a narrow temperature range; eurythermal ones tolerate a wide range.

s: Herbivores occupy which trophic level?
x: Herbivores are on the second level; top carnivores occupy the highest.

s: With which of the following does a detritus food chain begin?
x: Detritus chains begin with dead organic matter; grazing chains begin with living green plants.

s: A food chain that begins with leaf litter and passes through earthworms to birds is which type of food chain?
x: A detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter such as leaf litter and proceeds through detritivores such as earthworms to higher consumers.

s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence in an aquatic food chain?
o: Zooplankton → phytoplankton → large fish → small fish
Large fish → small fish → zooplankton → phytoplankton
Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish
Small fish → phytoplankton → zooplankton → large fish
x: Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are primary consumers, and small and large fish occupy progressively higher trophic positions.

s: Which of the following does NOT occupy the first trophic level?
x: Zooplankton are primary consumers at the second level; phytoplankton, seaweeds and green plants are producers.

s: With which of the following is DDT contamination in aquatic food chains most directly associated?
o: Thinning of bird eggshells and crashes in seabird populations
x: DDT causes thinning of bird eggshells and has been associated with crashes in seabird populations.

s: Why is an ecosystem with a more complex food web generally more stable?
o: It has more alternative feeding pathways
It eliminates all competition among organisms
x: A complex food web provides alternative pathways for energy and feeding relationships, increasing ecosystem stability.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ecosystem stability?
o: Resistance is the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance
Returning to the earlier condition after a forest fire shows resilience
Homeostasis is self-regulation through feedback up to a limit
Resistance is the ability to withstand a disturbance without change
x: Recovering after a disturbance is resilience; resistance is withstanding it without change.

s: Which one of the following ecosystems is generally the most stable?
x: Diverse and complex systems such as rainforests are generally more stable than simple systems such as tundra, deserts and monoculture croplands.

s: Why does ocean acidification pose a direct threat to marine ecosystems?
o: Weakens calcifying plankton and corals, thereby affecting marine food webs
Increases the salinity of freshwater ecosystems
Stops all forms of photosynthesis in the oceans
Strengthens the shells of calcifying plankton and corals
x: Ocean acidification weakens calcifying plankton and corals. Since these organisms occupy important positions in marine food webs, the effects can cascade through the ecosystem.

s: In the sequence ‘tiger, grass, snake, frog’, which trophic level is missing?
x: Grass represents the first trophic level and the remaining animals are consumers. The second trophic level, occupied by herbivores or primary consumers, is absent.

s: Which one of the following represents a grassland food chain mentioned in ecological examples?
o: Grass → grasshopper or rabbit → snake or hawk
x: A grassland chain begins with grass, followed by herbivores such as grasshoppers or rabbits, and then predators such as snakes or hawks.

s: What is the build-up of a pollutant within one organism over its life called?
x: Bioaccumulation is build-up within one organism; biomagnification is the rise in concentration at successive higher trophic levels.

s: What is the functional position occupied by an organism in a food chain called?
x: A trophic level is the functional position of an organism in a food chain; a species may occupy more than one level.

s: Minamata disease, first reported in Japan, was caused by biomagnification of which pollutant?
x: Methylmercury concentrated up the marine food chain and caused Minamata disease in Japan. DDT is linked to eggshell thinning in fish-eating birds; PCBs are another persistent biomagnifying pollutant but not the cause of Minamata disease; cadmium is not the cause either (it is associated with itai-itai disease).

s: Which of the following pollutants undergoes biomagnification along food chains?
x: Mercury builds up along food chains (biomagnification).

s: Which one of the following is the most appropriate set of characteristics of a pollutant that biomagnifies?
o: Radioactive, gaseous and readily converted into oxygen
Highly soluble in water, biodegradable and short-lived
x: Only persistent, fat-soluble and non-biodegradable pollutants are identified as biomagnifying pollutants in this context.

s: Which of the following pair consists entirely of secondary pollutants?
x: PAN and smog are both secondary pollutants, formed in the air. CO, SO₂ and NOx are primary.

s: What is the self-regulation of an ecosystem up to a limit through feedback called?
x: Homeostasis is self-regulation through feedback; resilience is recovery, resistance is withstanding disturbance.

s: What is the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance called?
x: Resilience is recovery after disturbance; resistance is withstanding it (APPSC 2024).

s: Secondary consumers occupy which trophic level?
x: Producers are 1st, primary consumers 2nd, secondary consumers 3rd and top carnivores 4th.

s: Lichens are commonly used as indicators of which of the following?
x: Lichens can indicate environmental health and are particularly used as indicators of sulphur dioxide pollution.

s: Why is the sea star Pisaster ochraceus regarded as a keystone species?
x: Pisaster ochraceus is a keystone sea star that controls mussels in intertidal zones. This example is associated with the work of Robert Paine.

s: Which one of the following is a foundation species?
x: Foundation species create or shape the habitat itself; corals and kelp are examples.

s: Which pair is NOT correctly matched?
o: Keystone species — effect much larger than its abundance
Umbrella species — attracts public support mainly through charisma
Foundation species — creates or shapes habitat
x: Attracting public support through charisma is the role of a flagship species. An umbrella species is wide-ranging, and its protection benefits many other species.

s: The association between a fig tree and a fig wasp is an example of which interaction?
x: The fig wasp pollinates the fig and obtains a breeding site, making the association a coevolved mutualistic relationship.

s: The relationship between a tiger and a deer is an example of which interaction?
x: Tiger and deer illustrate predation, not competition.

s: A large tree shading a small plant is an example of which interaction?
x: It is amensalism (-/0); a lichen is mutualism and the cattle egret near cattle is commensalism.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
x: Neutralism denotes an interaction in which neither species is significantly affected, represented by 0/0. Amensalism is -/0, predation is +/- and commensalism is +/0.

s: Which of the following pairs is associated with sexual deceit during pollination?
x: The Ophrys orchid attracts bees through sexual deceit, thereby facilitating pollination.

s: What is a wide-ranging species whose protection also protects many other species called?
x: An umbrella species, such as the tiger or snow leopard, is wide-ranging, so protecting it protects many others.

s: What is a charismatic species such as the giant panda, used to draw public support for conservation, called?
x: Flagship species are charismatic and draw support; keystone species have effects far larger than their numbers.

s: The cattle egret feeding near grazing cattle is an example of which interaction?
x: It is commensalism (+/0): the egret benefits while the cattle are unaffected.

s: Penicillium inhibiting other microbes is an example of which interaction?
x: Amensalism is −/0: one is harmed, the other unaffected; commensalism is +/0.

s: Which of the following is a coevolved plant-pollinator pair?
x: The yucca plant is pollinated only by the yucca moth; the two have coevolved, like the fig and fig wasp.

s: The association between fungi and the roots of plants in mycorrhiza is an example of which interaction?
x: In mycorrhiza both gain: the fungus helps the root absorb water and minerals such as phosphorus, and the plant feeds the fungus.

s: Gause's exclusion principle is related to which type of interaction?
x: Gause's competitive exclusion principle applies to competition (-/-) between species for the same limited resource.

s: What do all the populations of different species living in an area together form?
x: That is a community; a biome is a large region defined by climate and dominant vegetation.

s: In the ecological order from smallest to largest, which level comes immediately after population?
x: The order is organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere, so community follows population.

s: Which one of the following is regarded as the basic functional unit of ecology?
x: The ecosystem - a biotic community plus its non-living surroundings linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling - is the basic functional unit of ecology (APPSC PYQ). A population is one species in an area; a biome is a large climatic-vegetation region; the biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems.

s: What is the breaking of a continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches called?
x: Habitat fragmentation breaks continuous habitat into small isolated patches.

s: To qualify as a biodiversity hotspot, a region must have lost at least what share of its original habitat?
x: A hotspot must have at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and must have lost at least 70% of its original habitat.

s: Ramdeo Misra is popularly known as which of the following?
x: Ramdeo Misra is recognised as the father of Indian ecology.

s: Who coined the term 'biosphere'?
x: Eduard Suess coined 'biosphere' (1875); Tansley coined 'ecosystem' and Dasmann 'biological diversity'.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Grinnell proposed the habitat niche concept in 1917. Elton is associated with the functional niche, while Hutchinson proposed the n-dimensional niche.

s: Which of the following ecologists is wrongly matched?
o: A.G. Tansley – Coined the term ecosystem
H.C. Cowles – Succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes
F.E. Clements – Coined the term ecosystem
x: Clements is known for phases of succession and the monoclimax theory; Tansley coined 'ecosystem'.

s: Nutrients, water and air form which component of the environment?
x: Nutrients, water and air form the physical component; carbon and nitrogen cycles are its chemical interactions.

s: Which of the following is included in the cultural category of the environment?
x: The cultural environment is man-made and includes social, economic and political aspects.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a primary function of the environment?
x: The primary functions of the environment are providing resources, assimilating wastes and serving as a habitat for biodiversity. Generating synthetic chemicals is not one of them (APPSC 2024 trap).

s: Microbes belong to which category of the environment?
x: Microbes are living organisms and so biotic; lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere form the physical category.

s: Which of the following may exist even in the absence of life?
x: A habitat always has life and suits a particular species, whereas the environment may exist without life.

s: Who wrote the book *Animal Ecology* and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers?
x: Charles Elton wrote *Animal Ecology* in 1927 and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers.

s: Who studied ecological succession on the sand dunes of Lake Michigan?
x: H.C. Cowles studied succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes in 1899 (APPSC 2024 key).

s: Who is the author of the book Fundamentals of Ecology (1953)?
x: Fundamentals of Ecology is by E.P. Odum, father of modern ecosystem ecology, not E. Lucy Braun.

s: Who coined the term 'ecology' in 1866?
x: Ernst Haeckel coined 'ecology' in 1866; Tansley coined 'ecosystem' in 1935.

s: Who coined the term 'biological diversity'?
x: The term 'biological diversity' was coined by Raymond F. Dasmann.

s: Which of the following defines a biome?
o: A large region marked by its climate and dominant vegetation
Individuals of one species in an area
A transition zone where two communities meet
All the ecosystems of the Earth together
x: A biome, such as tundra, desert or rainforest, is a large region defined by climate and dominant vegetation.

s: To qualify as a biodiversity hotspot, at least how many endemic species of vascular plants must a region have?
x: A hotspot must have at least 1,500 endemic vascular plants and must have lost at least 70% of its original habitat.

s: Who proposed the concept of biodiversity hotspots?
x: Norman Myers gave the hotspot concept, later adopted by Conservation International.

s: Who proposed the n-dimensional niche concept in 1957?
x: G.E. Hutchinson described the niche as an n-dimensional space (1957); Grinnell gave the habitat niche and Elton the functional niche.

s: Alpha, beta and gamma are measures of which of the following?
x: Biodiversity is measured at three levels: alpha, beta and gamma diversity.

s: Which of the following is correct about habitat and environment?
o: A habitat can contain only one species
Habitat is a broader concept than environment
x: A habitat is a particular place within the broader environment, so all habitats are environments; one habitat may contain many species.

s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: Anthropogenic biome – Movement of nutrient elements through ecosystem components
Global hectare – Unit of ecological footprint
Biogeochemical cycle – Movement of nutrient elements through ecosystem components
Ecological footprint – Human demand on Earth's ecosystems
x: An anthropogenic biome (anthrome) is a human-altered terrestrial biosphere; nutrient movement is a biogeochemical cycle.

s: What does the edge effect in an ecotone refer to?
o: fewer species than either adjoining community
only species from the larger adjoining community
more species and higher density of some species than either adjoining community
x: The edge effect is the increased number of species and increased density of some species in an ecotone. Such organisms are called edge species.

s: Gloger’s rule primarily explains variation in which of the following characteristics in relation to climate?
x: Gloger’s rule relates climate to colouration; warm and humid environments are generally associated with darker colouration.

s: Which term refers to the transition zone between two ecosystems or communities?
x: An ecotone is the transition zone where two communities meet, such as a grassland between forest and desert. Lentic means still water, a sere is the whole sequence of communities in succession, and an anthrome is a human-altered biome.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Hydrophytes live in water; xerophytes live in deserts, halophytes in saline places and epiphytes on other plants.

s: Which of the following is NOT a typical adaptation of desert flora?
o: Broad, thin leaves that increase water loss
x: Desert plants commonly have deep roots, small or spiny leaves and waxy cuticles. Broad, thin leaves would generally increase water loss.

s: What are plants that send deep roots down to groundwater called?
x: Phreatophytes have deep roots reaching groundwater; hydrophytes have buoyant aerenchyma.

s: Jordan's ecogeographic rule relates temperature to which of the following?
x: Jordan's rule links colder conditions with more vertebrae in fish; Bergmann concerns body size, Allen appendages and Gloger colouration.

s: Which of the following is a stem parasite?
x: Cuscuta is a stem parasite; Nepenthes is insectivorous.

s: A thick cuticle, sunken stomata and CAM are features of which group of plants?
x: These are xerophyte (desert) features; hydrophytes have a thin cuticle, aerenchyma, reduced roots and floating leaves.

s: Hydrilla is an example of which of the following?
x: Hydrilla is an aquatic plant (hydrophyte); Opuntia is a xerophyte and Rhizophora a halophyte.

s: Which ecogeographic rule relates colder climates with shorter ears and limbs?
x: Allen's rule concerns appendage length; Bergmann's concerns body size and Rensch's sexual size dimorphism.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Uniform forest stand — ecotone between two communities
Estuary — fresh water and salt water interface
x: A uniform stand of one forest type is a single community, not an ecotone. Mangroves, estuaries and riverbanks represent the stated transition zones.

s: Between which of the following do mangroves form an ecotone?
x: Mangroves lie between marine and terrestrial ecosystems; a grassland is an ecotone between forest and desert.

s: On which of the following do lithophytes grow?
x: Lithophytes grow on rocks; hydrophytes grow in water and epiphytes on other plants for support.

s: Rhizophora, a mangrove plant growing on saline coasts, is an example of which group of plants?
x: Rhizophora grows in saline coastal soil, so it is a halophyte.

s: Which of the following are adaptations of halophytes?
x: Halophytes such as mangroves have breathing roots (pneumatophores), vivipary and salt glands.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Rule)
A. Bergmann's rule
B. Allen's rule
C. Gloger's rule
List-II (Trait)
1. Colouration
2. Body size
3. Length of ears and limbs
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Bergmann's rule is about body size, Allen's about ears and limbs, and Gloger's about colouration.

s: A grassland forms an ecotone between which of the following?
x: Grassland is a transition zone between forest and desert; an estuary lies between fresh and salt water and mangroves between marine and terrestrial.

s: What is gross primary productivity minus producer respiration called?
x: NPP is GPP minus producer respiration; secondary productivity is new organic matter formed by consumers.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ecosystem productivity?
o: Primary productivity is at the autotroph level
Mangroves are among the most productive ecosystems
Secondary productivity is at the autotroph level
Open oceans are among the least productive ecosystems
x: Secondary productivity is at the consumer (heterotroph) level.

s: What is the nature of energy flow in an ecosystem?
x: Energy flows in one direction and obeys the laws of thermodynamics; nutrients, not energy, are cycled.

s: Why do food chains generally not extend beyond four or five trophic levels?
o: Energy is recycled back to producers
About 90% of energy is lost at each trophic transfer
Producers capture about 10% of incoming solar energy
x: About 90% of energy is lost at each transfer through respiration, excretion, locomotion and heat, leaving too little for many levels.

s: As energy passes from one trophic level to the next, in which form is most of the energy not transferred lost?
x: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level; the rest is lost, largely as heat, so energy decreases upward.

s: What is the average total primary production efficiency of an ecosystem, as a share of incoming solar energy?
x: Only about 1–2% of incoming solar energy is captured in photosynthesis; 10% is the share passed between trophic levels.

s: Which one of the following ecosystems is generally the most productive in terms of net primary productivity per unit area?
x: Tropical rainforests are the standard highest-productivity ecosystem among the alternatives. Estuaries, coral reefs and swamps also have high productivity.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about oceanic productivity?
o: Open oceans have low net primary productivity per unit area
The total output of oceans is large because of their extensive area
Tropical rainforests are more productive per unit area than open oceans
Oceans are the most productive ecosystems per unit area
x: Per unit area, open oceans are low in productivity; tropical rainforests and some aquatic ecosystems are more productive.

s: About how much energy is transferred when energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
x: Only about 10% of energy passes upward, so energy decreases at each level and flows one way.

s: Who gave the ten percent law of energy transfer?
x: Raymond Lindeman proposed the ten percent law in 1942.

s: Which law explains the loss of energy as heat at each trophic transfer?
x: The second law says each energy transfer loses heat; the first law says energy is transformed, not destroyed.

s: Plants fix about what share of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)?
x: Plants fix about 2-10% of PAR, while total primary production efficiency is about 1-2% of incoming solar energy.

s: Where is the AP State Biodiversity Board planning Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs)?
o: Inside all urban municipal limits only
x: The AP State Biodiversity Board is planning OECMs outside protected areas as part of broader conservation efforts.

s: Which one of the following does NOT belong to marine ecosystems?
x: Rivers are freshwater ecosystems. Coral reefs, hydrothermal vents and tidal zones are marine ecosystems.

s: Which of the following pairs of Indian estuaries is located on the west coast?
x: Narmada and Tapi are major west-coast estuaries. Hooghly, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery are east-coast estuaries.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Freshwater — open oceans and shallow seas
Marine water — coral reefs and open oceans
Brackish water — estuaries and mangrove swamps
x: Open oceans and shallow seas are marine ecosystems, not freshwater ecosystems. Springs and rivers are lotic freshwater examples, while lakes and ponds are lentic examples.

s: Which lake zone is characterised by shallow water, light reaching the bottom and rooted plants?
x: The littoral zone is the shallow edge of a lake where light reaches the bottom and rooted plants commonly grow.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the profundal zone of a lake?
o: Deep, dark water below the limnetic zone with decomposers
Sunlit open water dominated by plankton
x: The profundal zone lies below the limnetic zone, is deep and dark, does not support photosynthesis, and is associated with decomposers.

s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: Pulicat – Brackish-water lagoon on the AP–Tamil Nadu border
Kolleru – Brackish-water lagoon on the AP–Tamil Nadu border
Coringa – Mangrove-estuary wildlife sanctuary in the Godavari delta
Eastern Ghats – Tropical forests grading into thorn forests on the Rayalaseema plateau
x: Kolleru is a freshwater lake between the Godavari and Krishna deltas; the brackish lagoon is Pulicat.

s: Ponds, lakes and swamps are examples of which of the following?
x: Ponds, lakes and swamps are lentic (still water); rivers and streams are lotic (flowing water).

s: What is the salinity of freshwater?
x: Freshwater has salinity below 5 ppt; brackish water is 5–35 ppt and marine water 35 ppt or more.

s: Which of the following are features of eutrophic lakes?
x: Eutrophic lakes are nutrient-rich and may develop algal blooms; oxygen at depth is often low.

s: What is the open water column of the ocean called?
x: The open water column is the pelagic zone; the benthic zone is the sea floor and its organisms.

s: Which of the following are functions of wetlands?
o: Water purification and carbon storage only
Flood moderation, water purification, biodiversity conservation and carbon storage
x: Wetlands moderate floods, purify water, conserve biodiversity and store carbon.

s: In which year did India become a party to the Ramsar Convention?
x: India joined in 1982; the Convention was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran.

s: The Nallamala and Seshachalam forests are part of which of the following?
x: Nallamala and Seshachalam are Eastern Ghats forests that provide habitat for tigers, leopards, sloth bears and elephants.

s: Which of the following is NOT a climate-resilience function of mangroves?
o: Increasing the salinity of all freshwater lakes
x: Mangroves buffer cyclones and storm surges, reduce coastal erosion and store carbon. They do not increase the salinity of all freshwater lakes.

s: What is the usual salinity near the sea-facing mouth of an estuary?
x: Estuary salinity rises from near-freshwater upstream to about 35 ppt at the mouth.

s: Wetlands in India are specifically protected under which of the following?
x: The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 provide the specific legal framework for wetland protection in India.

s:
Assertion (A): Coral reefs are called the 'rainforests of the sea'.
Reason (R): Coral reefs break storm waves and prevent coastal erosion.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true, but the 'rainforest' label rests on the reefs' very high species richness, not on their coastal-protection role.

s: On which date is World Wetlands Day observed?
x: The Ramsar Convention was signed on 2 February 1971, which is observed as World Wetlands Day.

s: Which of the following is a coastal wetland rather than an inland wetland?
x: Lagoons, estuaries and mangroves are coastal wetlands. Lakes, marshes and floodplains are inland wetlands.

s: Which ocean zone lies below about 1,000 m and is dark?
x: The aphotic zone lies below ~1,000 m; the disphotic is ~200-1,000 m twilight and the photic the upper ~200 m.

s: What is the sea floor zone of the ocean called?
x: The benthic zone is the sea floor; the pelagic is the open water column.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Coringa is a mangrove estuary in the Godavari delta; Kolleru is freshwater and Pulicat a brackish lagoon.

s: What type of water body is Kolleru, between the Godavari and Krishna deltas?
x: Kolleru is a freshwater lake and Ramsar site; Pulicat is brackish and Coringa a mangrove estuary.

s: Which state has the largest wetland area in India?
x: Gujarat has the largest wetland area, about 17.6%.

s: Where was the Ramsar Convention on wetlands signed in 1971?
x: The convention was signed on 2 February 1971 at Ramsar in Iran, hence its name.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Ramsar Convention:
1. It imposes punitive sanctions on countries that damage listed wetlands.
2. India became a party to it in 1982.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Ramsar Convention is not regulatory and has no punitive sanctions; India joined it in 1982.

s: The 'Montreux Record' is associated with which international convention?
x: The Montreux Record is kept under the Ramsar Convention on wetlands; it lists sites whose ecological character is threatened.

s: Which type of lake has low nutrients and clear water?
x: Oligotrophic lakes are low in nutrients and clear; eutrophic lakes are nutrient-rich with algal blooms.

s: What is the length of the coastline of Andhra Pradesh?
x: Andhra Pradesh has a coastline of 1,053 km.

s: What does the fundamental niche of a species refer to?
o: the actual range occupied after competition
the full range of conditions and resources it could use in the absence of other species
x: Fundamental niche is the potential range of conditions and resources available to a species when competition and other biological limitations are absent.

s: A koala feeds mainly on eucalyptus. Which of the following describes it?
x: A specialist uses a narrow range of resources. Dependence of the koala mainly on eucalyptus is an example of narrow niche breadth.

s: What is the functional role ('profession') of a species in its habitat called?
x: The niche is a species' functional role; it is unique to each species.

s: Which of the following is NOT a population attribute?
x: Density, mortality, age structure and sex ratio are population attributes. Dominant vegetation is associated with the description of a biome.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Mortality — births per female per unit time
Carrying capacity — number of predators only
x: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area. Mortality refers to deaths per unit time, while natality refers to births.

s: Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched?
x: A triangular age pyramid indicates an expanding population. Bell-shaped and urn-shaped pyramids indicate stable and declining populations respectively.

s: When can competing species coexist?
o: avoid all interaction with other species
use different parts or forms of a shared resource
x: Resource partitioning permits competing species to coexist by using different portions of a resource, such as different parts of the same plant.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about population growth?
o: A J-shaped curve shows growth that levels off at carrying capacity
Carrying capacity is the maximum population an environment can sustain
A J-shaped curve shows exponential growth with unlimited resources
An S-shaped curve shows logistic growth levelling off at carrying capacity K
x: The J-curve is exponential growth (dN/dt = rN); levelling off at K belongs to the S-curve.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about r-selected and K-selected species?
o: K-selected species produce few large offspring with considerable parental care
Elephants and humans commonly show K-selected characteristics
x: Weeds, like insects, commonly show r-selected characteristics.

s: What kind of population does an urn-shaped age pyramid indicate?
x: Triangular pyramids show expanding, bell-shaped stable and urn-shaped declining populations.

s: Which curve does exponential population growth under unlimited resources produce?
x: The J-curve is exponential growth (dN/dt = rN); the S-curve is logistic growth levelling at carrying capacity K.

s:
Consider the following statements about r- and K-selected species:
1. r-selected species such as insects and weeds produce many small offspring with little care.
2. K-selected species typically live in unstable habitats.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 1 is correct; K-selected species (elephants, humans) live long near carrying capacity, while unstable habitats suit r-selected species.

s: What is the term for the rate of birth of individuals in a population, expressed per unit population per unit time?
x: Natality is the birth of individuals in a population; its rate is given per unit population per unit time (or, in many texts, per female per unit time). Mortality is deaths and density is individuals per unit area.

s: What is the largest population that an environment can support for ever called?
x: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can sustain; the S-curve levels off at it (K).

s: What is the actual range of conditions and resources used by a species under competition called?
x: The realised niche is the part of the fundamental niche a species actually uses when competitors are present.

s: Why can the biomass pyramid in an aquatic ecosystem be inverted?
o: Fish do not consume zooplankton in aquatic ecosystems.
Energy increases at every aquatic trophic level.
Phytoplankton have a small standing crop but rapidly support larger zooplankton and fish biomass.
x: Phytoplankton have a small standing crop but reproduce and are consumed rapidly, allowing them to support a larger standing biomass of zooplankton and fish.

s: Which of the following statements regarding ecological pyramids is correct?
o: The base represents top consumers and the apex represents producers.
The base generally represents producers and the apex represents top consumers.
Ecological pyramids have only two types.
All organisms occupy only one trophic level.
x: The base of an ecological pyramid represents producers and the apex represents top consumers. The three types are pyramids of number, biomass and energy.

s: Which organisms receive no place in ecological pyramids despite their vital role?
x: Ecological pyramids omit saprophytes and decomposers; they also cannot place one species at two trophic levels.

s: In which of the following may an inverted pyramid of numbers also occur?
o: a forest floor litter chain only
x: Parasitic food chains can have fewer hosts supporting numerous parasites, resulting in an inverted pyramid of numbers.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Pyramid of biomass – May be inverted in a tree ecosystem
Pyramid of energy – May be inverted in aquatic ecosystems
x: The energy pyramid is always upright; the number pyramid may be inverted in a tree ecosystem and the biomass pyramid in aquatic systems.

s: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of ecological pyramids?
o: They assume a simple food chain and ignore food webs
A species cannot be placed at two levels
Saprophytes and decomposers get no place
They cannot show producers at the base
x: Producers always form the base of a pyramid; the other three are its limitations.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The biomass pyramid in a forest is upright.
The biomass pyramid in a pond is inverted.
The biomass pyramid in a marine ecosystem is upright.
The biomass pyramid in a grassland is upright.
x: Option C is incorrect: in the sea the biomass pyramid is inverted, because a small mass of fast-growing phytoplankton supports more zooplankton. Forest and grassland pyramids are upright.

s: What is the living biomass present in a trophic level per unit area at a given time called?
x: Standing crop is the amount of living biomass at a given time; productivity, by contrast, is a rate.

s: In which of the following is the pyramid of numbers inverted?
x: In a tree ecosystem one large tree supports many herbivores, so the pyramid of numbers is inverted; in grassland and pond it is upright.

s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Artificial or man-modified ecosystem — crop field
x: Crop fields are artificial or man-modified ecosystems. Forests, oceans, lakes, deserts and grasslands are natural ecosystems, while a city is an extreme artificial example.

s: India launched its first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems at which international event and venue?
x: India launched its first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems at UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar.

s: Which of the following are features of taiga (boreal) forests?
o: Slow decay, thick litter and acidic soil
Thin, nutrient-poor soil due to fast decay
Fast decay and highly fertile soil
x: Taiga has slow decay, thick litter and acidic soil; fast decay and thin, poor soil mark tropical rainforests.

s: Open Natural Ecosystems cover over 10% of India, but what share of them is protected?
x: Open Natural Ecosystems cover more than 10% of India, but less than 5% of them are protected.

s: Which of the following is NOT a natural terrestrial ecosystem?
x: Tundra, forest, grassland, desert and mountain are terrestrial ecosystems; an estuary is aquatic.

s: Why do mature forests provide little net oxygen?
o: They are no longer carbon sinks
x: In mature forests respiration roughly balances photosynthesis, though they remain important carbon sinks.

s: Which of the following is a cold desert?
x: Ladakh and the Gobi are cold deserts; the Thar of western Rajasthan and Kutch is a hot desert.

s: Steppe is the temperate grassland of which region?
x: Steppe is the Eurasian temperate grassland; Australia's grasslands are the Downs.

s: Where do Shola grasslands occur?
o: Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha
Himalayan foothills of Uttarakhand and Assam
Western Ghats of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
x: Shola occurs in the Western Ghats; the tall wet Terai grasslands lie along the Himalayan foothills.

s: Which is the main invasive threat to the Banni grassland of Kutch?
x: The invasive threat named for Banni is Prosopis juliflora, not Lantana camara.

s: Which forest ecosystem generally has the highest species richness on land?
x: Tropical rainforests have the highest species richness among terrestrial ecosystems.

s: Where is the Veld grassland found?
x: Veld is in South Africa; Prairie is North America, Pampas Argentina and Downs Australia.

s: Which of the following is a hot desert in India?
x: Thar (western Rajasthan, Kutch) is a hot desert; Ladakh and Gobi are cold deserts.

s: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the taiga (boreal coniferous) forest?
x: The tropical rainforest, not the taiga, has the highest species richness on land; taiga has slow decay, thick litter and acidic soil.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Grassland)
A. Prairie
B. Pampas
C. Downs
D. Steppe
List-II (Region)
1. Australia
2. Eurasia
3. North America
4. Argentina
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Prairie is in North America, Pampas in Argentina, Downs in Australia and Steppe in Eurasia.

s: Downs are the temperate grasslands of which country?
x: Downs are in Australia; Pampas are in Argentina and Veld in South Africa.

s: Which biofertiliser fixes nitrogen as a free-living organism?
x: Azotobacter fixes nitrogen free-living, whereas Rhizobium fixes it symbiotically in legume root nodules.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding denitrification is correct?
o: It converts nitrate into nitrogen gas and returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.
It converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia in root nodules.
It converts organic nitrogen into ammonia through decomposition.
It converts ammonia into nitrite in the presence of Nitrosomonas.
x: Denitrification converts nitrate into nitrogen gas, thereby returning nitrogen to the atmosphere. Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus are associated with this process.

s: Which of the following processes directly converts organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia?
x: Ammonification is the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia by decomposer bacteria and fungi.

s: Which microorganisms are associated with the two stages of nitrification respectively?
x: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrite, while Nitrobacter converts nitrite into nitrate.

s: With which plants does Frankia, a symbiotic actinomycete, fix nitrogen?
o: Non-legumes such as Alnus and Casuarina
x: Frankia forms symbiotic associations with non-legumes such as Alnus and Casuarina.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Azolla — aquatic fern associated with Anabaena and useful for nitrogen supply in paddy
Mycorrhiza — free-living aerobic bacterium for non-legumes
Blue-green algae — fungus-root association for phosphorus uptake
PSB — aquatic fern used only in flooded rice fields
x: Azolla is an aquatic fern associated with Anabaena and supplies nitrogen in paddy systems. The other pairs confuse the functions or types of biofertilisers.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Azotobacter is associated with free-living nitrogen fixation.
Anabaena is a symbiont of Azotobacter.
Lactobacillus is associated with curd formation.
Cyanobacteria perform photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation.
x: Option B is incorrect: Anabaena lives in the leaves of the water fern Azolla, not with Azotobacter, which is free-living. The other statements are right.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Rhizobium japonicum lives in soybean nodules; Rhizobium lives in legume nodules, Azotobacter is free-living and Anabaena lives in Azolla.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Rhizobium – Symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume root nodules
Anabaena – Lives in the leaf cavities of the fern Azolla
Cyanobacteria – Symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume root nodules
x: Cyanobacteria are the group of photosynthetic blue-green algae that fix nitrogen; symbiotic fixation in legume nodules is done by Rhizobium.

s: How do phosphate-solubilising microbes act as biofertilisers?
x: Phosphate-solubilising microbes release bound phosphorus, adding nutrients and promoting growth.

s: What is the principal function of leg-haemoglobin in legume root nodules?
o: Maintaining suitable oxygen conditions for nitrogen fixation
x: Leghaemoglobin binds oxygen to keep its level low in nodules, because nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
x: Bacillus megaterium is a phosphate solubiliser (PSB), so A is right. Pseudomonas striata is also a phosphate solubiliser, not linked to nitrogenase (used in nitrogen fixation); VAM aids phosphorus and water uptake, not denitrification; Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate in nitrification, not phosphate uptake.

s:
Consider the following statements about the nitrogen cycle:
1. Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrite.
2. Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate.
3. Denitrification adds usable nitrogen to the soil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Nitrification runs Nitrosomonas (to nitrite) then Nitrobacter (to nitrate); denitrification removes nitrogen, returning N₂ to the air.

s: What is the red or pink substance found in legume root nodules?
x: Leghaemoglobin is the pink pigment in legume root nodules, where symbiotic Rhizobium fixes nitrogen.

s: Which process removes nitrogen from the soil by returning it to the atmosphere as N₂ gas?
x: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere as N₂; fixation, ammonification and nitrification add usable nitrogen to soil.

s: In the uptake of which of the following does mycorrhiza, particularly VAM, mainly help plants?
x: VAM is a fungus-root association that improves phosphorus and water uptake by plants.

s: In rice fields, with which water fern does the cyanobacterium Anabaena live?
x: Anabaena lives in the aquatic fern Azolla; the Azolla-Anabaena pair is used in rice fields.

s: Which is the main reservoir of nitrogen in the nitrogen cycle?
x: About 78% of air is nitrogen gas, so the atmosphere, not the soil, is the main reservoir of nitrogen.

s: Apart from nitrogen-fixing organisms, which natural process fixes atmospheric nitrogen that reaches the soil with rain?
x: Lightning turns atmospheric nitrogen into compounds that rain carries to the soil, adding to its nitrogen.

s: Which bacteria carry out denitrification?
x: Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus turn nitrate back into nitrogen gas; Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter carry out nitrification.

s: Which enzyme carries out biological nitrogen fixation?
x: Nitrogenase converts atmospheric N2 into ammonia during nitrogen fixation.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The enzyme nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen.
2. Leghaemoglobin in legume root nodules keeps the oxygen level low.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen, so the pink pigment leghaemoglobin binds oxygen and keeps it low in the nodules.

s: In which specialised cells of blue-green algae does nitrogen fixation take place?
x: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) fix nitrogen in heterocysts, which is why they are used as biofertiliser in paddy.

s: Which industrial process fixes atmospheric nitrogen?
x: Besides organisms and lightning, nitrogen is fixed industrially by the Haber process (ammonia).

s: What is the ecosystem function of maintaining ecological balance known as?
x: Homeostasis is the maintenance of ecological balance; succession, nutrient cycling and energy flow are other ecosystem functions.

s: Which function of the environment does 'supply of drugs and herbal remedies' describe?
x: Supply of drugs and herbal remedies is medicinal resources; waste decomposition is the breakdown of organic waste into simpler compounds.

s: Protection from UV radiation by the ozone layer falls under which function of the environment?
x: Sustaining life includes genetic diversity, biodiversity and ozone's protection from UV radiation.

s: How does biodegradation contribute to the functioning of an ecosystem?
o: removing biodiversity from the food chain
converting organic waste into nutrients through microorganisms
x: Biodegradation recycles waste when microorganisms break down organic material and release nutrients. This makes nutrients available for reuse in the ecosystem.

s: Which of the following statements about the functions of the environment is NOT correct?
o: It sustains life through biodiversity and the ozone layer
It provides aesthetic services such as scenery
x: The environment supplies both renewable and non-renewable resources, so 'only renewable' is wrong.

s: How do nutrients in an ecosystem differ from energy?
o: flow only through the atmosphere and never through organisms
are consumed permanently and cannot return to the ecosystem
are recycled indefinitely, whereas energy is not
x: Nutrients are recycled through ecosystems, while energy flows through the system and is not recycled indefinitely.

s: Which one of the following combinations contains only processes that add carbon dioxide to the carbon cycle?
o: Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion and volcanic activity
Photosynthesis, ocean dissolution, carbonate sedimentation and silicate weathering
Photosynthesis, respiration, carbonate sedimentation and deforestation
Ocean dissolution, decomposition, silicate weathering and photosynthesis
x: Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion and volcanic activity all add CO2. Each other option includes a process that removes CO2: photosynthesis, dissolution in oceans, carbonate sedimentation or silicate weathering.

s: Which of the following removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
x: Silicate weathering, photosynthesis, ocean dissolution and carbonate sedimentation remove CO₂; the others add it.

s: Which of the following are long-term carbon reservoirs?
x: Long-term carbon reservoirs are carbonate rocks and fossil fuels.

s: Which of the following has a gaseous nutrient cycle?
x: Carbon and nitrogen have gaseous cycles, while phosphorus, sulphur and potassium have sedimentary cycles.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about decomposers?
o: Their removal would obstruct the movement of minerals in an ecosystem
They return nutrients locked in dead organic matter to the soil
They recycle energy back to the producers
They keep the biogeochemical cycles running
x: Decomposers recycle nutrients, not energy: energy flows through an ecosystem and is not recycled.

s: Which of the following nutrient cycles has no atmospheric phase?
x: The phosphorus cycle has no atmospheric phase; weathering releases phosphorus from rocks and much of it ends in ocean sediments.

s: What is the main reservoir of sedimentary cycles such as phosphorus and sulphur?
x: Sedimentary cycles (phosphorus, sulphur, calcium, potassium, iron) have the Earth's crust as main reservoir.

s: What would happen to mineral cycling if all decomposers were removed from an ecosystem?
o: Nutrients would stay locked in dead matter and not return to the soil
Energy would begin to cycle back to producers
Minerals would return to the soil faster
x: Decomposers break dead matter into simple nutrients; without them minerals stay locked in dead organisms.

s: How does seasonal succession differ from succession caused by a disturbance?
o: caused exclusively by the removal of soil
a permanent replacement ending only in a forest climax
a cyclic change driven by environmental rhythms
x: Seasonal succession is cyclical and is driven by environmental rhythms; it is not caused by a disaster or disturbance.

s: Compared with primary succession, how fast is secondary succession generally?
o: Slower, because no soil is present
Equally fast, because pioneers are the same
Faster, because soil, seeds or roots remain
Slower, because lichens must first form soil
x: Secondary succession follows destruction of an existing community where soil, seeds or roots remain, so it is faster.

s: What is ecological succession beginning on sand known as?
x: Psammosere begins on sand and, like lithosere (bare rock), is a sub-type of xerosere; halosere begins on saline soil or water.

s: In ecological succession, what is the stable final community in balance with the climate called?
x: The climax community is the stable terminal community related to the prevailing climate; pioneers colonise first and seral communities are intermediate.

s: What is succession that begins on bare rock called?
x: Lithosere starts on bare rock; psammosere on sand, halosere on saline soil or water.

s: What is succession beginning on saline soil or water called?
x: A halosere starts on saline soil or water.

s: In Frederic Clements' scheme of succession, which phase immediately follows nudation?
x: Clements' sequence is nudation, invasion, competition and co-action, reaction and stabilisation.

s: What does the term 'ecesis' in ecological succession refer to?
o: the final stabilisation of a climax community
the successful establishment of invading organisms
the seasonal disappearance of a community
the elimination of unfit species through competition
x: Ecesis is the successful establishment of organisms that have migrated into an area during the invasion phase.

s: In which of Clements' phases of succession do organisms modify soil, water, light and temperature?
x: Reaction, the most important phase, is when organisms modify soil, water, light and temperature, making the site suitable for later species.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about xerosere succession on bare rock?
o: Crustose lichens are the pioneers on bare rock
x: The sequence is crustose lichens, foliose lichens, mosses, herbs, shrubs and forest, so mosses come after foliose lichens, not before.

s: In a hydrosere, which stage comes immediately after the reed-swamp stage?
x: Hydrosere proceeds phytoplankton - submerged rooted plants - floating plants - reed-swamp - sedge-meadow - woodland - forest.

s: Why are hydroseres generally better studied than xeroseres?
o: Their climax communities are exclusively aquatic.
Lake sediments preserve a permanent record of their development.
They always contain more species than xeroseres.
They are unaffected by climatic changes.
x: Lake sediments preserve a permanent record of ecological changes, making hydroseres better studied than xeroseres.

s: Who proposed the polyclimax theory of ecological succession?
x: Tansley proposed polyclimax; Clements monoclimax and Whittaker climax-pattern.

s: With whom is the climax-pattern theory of succession associated?
x: Whittaker gave the climax-pattern theory; Clements monoclimax; Tansley polyclimax.

s: Which phase of Clements' succession is considered the most important?
x: Reaction, when organisms modify soil, water, light and temperature, is the most important phase.

s:
Which of the following is the correct sequence of Clements' phases of ecological succession?
1. Invasion
2. Nudation
3. Stabilisation
4. Reaction
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Succession starts with nudation (bare area), then invasion, competition, reaction and finally stabilisation (climax).

s: Which is the first stage of a hydrosere?
x: A hydrosere starts with phytoplankton, then submerged rooted plants, floating plants, reed-swamp, sedge-meadow, woodland and forest.

s: Under the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, soil formation is classified as which type of service?
x: Soil formation is a supporting service; food and water are provisioning, climate regulation is regulating and recreation is cultural.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a provisioning ecosystem service under the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment classification?
x: Pollination is a regulating service. Timber, medicinal resources and fresh water are provisioning services.

s: Which of the following forest benefits is an ecological service rather than an economic product?
x: Groundwater recharge and flood moderation are ecological services; timber and bamboo are economic products from forests.

s: Which category of ecosystem services is most difficult to express in monetary terms, causing their value to be underestimated?
x: Cultural services such as spiritual value, heritage and aesthetics are hard to price, so monetary estimates understate total value.

s: Which of the following is an intangible ecosystem service provided by forests in Andhra Pradesh?
x: AP forests act as carbon sinks, regulate water flow and conserve soil and moisture - intangible services beyond market-priced goods.

s: At about what value did Costanza and his associates first value global ecosystem services in 1997?
x: Costanza et al. estimated the annual value of global ecosystem services at approximately US$33 trillion in 1997.

s: Which organisation hosts TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity)?
x: TEEB was launched in 2007 at Potsdam in the G8+5 context and is hosted by UNEP; it seeks to make nature's values visible in decisions.

s: With which of the following is EnviStats India, compiled annually by MoSPI, associated?
o: Only the enumeration of endangered species
Assessment of atmospheric nitrogen fixation by legumes
Natural capital accounting under the UN SEEA framework
x: EnviStats India is an annual MoSPI compilation of environmental-economic accounts under the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting framework.

s: Where was The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity (TEEB) launched in 2007?
x: TEEB was launched in 2007 at Potsdam in the G8+5 context and is hosted by UNEP.

s: In which year did the UN release the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment?
x: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) grouped ecosystem services into four categories.

s: What does fertiliser runoff into water bodies most directly lead to?
x: Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms; their decay uses up dissolved oxygen, producing eutrophication and dead zones.

s: Why has Prosopis juliflora been described as an 'ecological first responder'?
o: Forms the final climax community in every ecosystem
Spreads when hydrology and soil chemistry have changed
Prevents all invasive species from establishing
Fixes nitrogen exclusively in rice fields
x: The invasive Prosopis juliflora spreads in response to changes in hydrology and soil chemistry, leading to its description as an ecological first responder.

s: Human activity has at least ____ the nitrogen available to plants.
x: Nitrogen overload: human activity has at least doubled nitrogen available to plants.

s: Nitrogen fertiliser in soil leads microbes to release which greenhouse gas?
x: Microbes release nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, from nitrogen fertiliser in soil.

s: The decay of algal blooms caused by fertiliser runoff uses up dissolved oxygen and creates which of the following?
x: Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms; their decay uses up dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones.

s: Why do wetlands act as microclimate regulators?
o: Evaporates and moderates local temperature and humidity
Blocks sunlight from reaching the ground
x: The water stored in wetlands evaporates and holds heat, moderating nearby temperature and humidity.

s: Which ecosystem acts as a sponge by storing floodwater, recharging aquifers and sustaining lean-season flow?
x: Wetlands store floodwater, recharge aquifers and sustain lean-season flow.

s: Which one of the following is a function of wetlands?
x: Wetlands control erosion, retain sediment, support nutrient cycling and support biodiversity.

s: What are the main causes of desertification in semi-arid regions?
o: low population pressure and regular rainfall
x: Overgrazing and deforestation are identified as the main causes of desertification in semi-arid regions.

s: With which of the following are salinisation and waterlogging mainly associated?
x: Poor drainage and over-irrigation cause salinisation and waterlogging, including in delta regions.

s: Which of the following pairs (process – effect) is correctly matched?
o: Wind erosion – Rivers and reservoirs receive sediment
Wind erosion – Vegetation cover is stripped
Water erosion – Topsoil is blown away in dry areas
x: Overgrazing strips vegetation; water erosion removes topsoil and causes sedimentation, and wind erosion blows topsoil away in dry areas.

s: In which States has excess urea skewed the NPK ratio of soils?
x: Excess use of urea has skewed the nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium balance in the soils of Punjab and Haryana.

s: Which of the following pairs (resource depletion – cause) is correctly matched?
x: Groundwater is depleted by over-irrigation; topsoil by erosion from overgrazing and deforestation, habitats by deforestation, land by salinity and waterlogging.

s: By 2050, salinisation and waterlogging could affect about what share of the world's arable land?
x: Salinisation and waterlogging from over-irrigation and poor drainage could affect 50% of world arable land by 2050.

s: What does desertification mean?
o: the conversion of all forests into agricultural land
the spread of existing deserts alone into neighbouring regions
the natural formation of sand dunes only
land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities
x: Desertification involves land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas due to climatic variation and human activity; it is not merely the spread of existing deserts.

s: Which concept describes degradation caused by over-use of a shared pasture?
x: Over-use of a commonly shared pasture is described as the Tragedy of the Commons, a concept associated with Garrett Hardin in 1968.

s: Under the Watershed Development Component of PMKSY, watershed development in India follows which approach?
x: Watershed development under the PMKSY Watershed Development Component follows the 'ridge to valley' approach, treating the upper catchment first and moving downstream. The other options are not the stated approach.

s: In which year did Garrett Hardin propound the 'Tragedy of the Commons'?
x: Hardin's Tragedy of the Commons (1968) describes how over-use of a shared pasture lowers land quality.

s: By which year is Land Degradation Neutrality under SDG 15.3 to be achieved?
x: LDN means no net loss of land health by 2030 (SDG 15.3).

s: In 70 years, the organic carbon content of Indian soils fell from about 1% to what level?
x: Soil organic carbon in Indian soils fell from 1% to 0.3% in 70 years.

s: What is the full form of LDN, the target under SDG 15.3?
x: LDN means Land Degradation Neutrality, that is, no net loss of land health by 2030.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the Appiko Movement?
x: The Appiko Movement occurred in Karnataka in 1983 and was associated with Panduranga Hegde.

s: In which State did the Mitti Bachao movement of 1977 take place?
x: Mitti Bachao (1977) was in Madhya Pradesh against waterlogging and salinity; Appiko was in Karnataka.

s: Which of the following pairs (movement – leader) is correctly matched?
x: Chipko (1973) was led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna; Panduranga Hegde led Appiko (1983).

s: The Mitti Bachao movement protested against waterlogging and salinity caused by which dam?
x: Mitti Bachao arose around the Tawa dam in Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh.

s: In which village did Gaura Devi lead women to save trees during the Chipko movement in 1974?
x: Gaura Devi led the women of Reni village in Chamoli in 1974, a key event of the Chipko movement.

s: In which district of Uttarakhand did the Chipko movement begin in 1973?
x: The Chipko movement began in Chamoli district in 1973, led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna.

s: Why does deforestation add to the greenhouse effect?
o: raises soil fertility in all regions
reduces the carbon sink capacity of forests
x: Deforestation removes vegetation that acts as a carbon sink. The resulting loss of carbon absorption adds to the greenhouse effect.

s: Approximately what proportion of the Earth's land is covered by forests?
x: FAO FRA 2025 puts forests at about 32% of Earth's land. 54% is the share of world forests held by five countries (Russia, Brazil, Canada, USA, China); 21.76% and 25.17% are India's forest cover and forest-plus-tree cover in ISFR 2023.

s: Which five countries together hold more than 54% of the world's forests?
o: India, Brazil, Canada, Australia and China
Brazil, Canada, Australia, India and the United States
Russia, Brazil, Canada, the United States and China
Russia, India, the United States, Indonesia and China
x: Russia, Brazil, Canada, the United States and China together hold more than 54% of the world's forests.

s: As per older FAO FRA figures, annual net forest loss fell from 8.3 million ha in the 1990s to what level?
x: The older FRA figures record a decline from 8.3 million ha per year in the 1990s to 5.2 million ha per year during 2000–2010.

s: Which forest zones have the highest forest loss?
o: coniferous forests of Russia and Canada alone
tropical forests of the Amazon, Congo Basin and Southeast Asia
temperate forests of Europe and North America
mangrove forests of the Indian coastline alone
